question: For a simple undirected graph with N vertices given by its adjacency matrix A: (1) what does the entry (A^k)_{ij} represent, (2) how can one determine from A whether the graph is connected, and (3) what is the definition of a path between vertices n_i and n_j?

sources.title: Graph Theory (Գրաֆների տեսություն), study manual
sources.notes: Local file at repository root, not under sources/. Printed pages are PDF pages minus one; cited by printed page. Pages viewed as images: printed 11, 16, 21, 22, 23, 48, 49. Armenian quotes were transcribed from the page images (subscripts flattened, for example u0 for u with subscript 0). Textbook for a university course; primary for definitions and numbering. A text-layer search of all 216 PDF pages for the adjacency-matrix term hit printed pp. 7, 11, 12, 34, 61 only; only p. 11 was viewed; the others are as recorded in graph-sources.md and were not re-viewed in this run. The book has no walk-counting theorem and no matrix connectivity test, as far as that search shows.

sources.venue: University of Galway mathematics lecture notes, Chapter 1
sources.notes: Downloaded and read all 7 pages as text. File names no author and no date; the URL path is not an authorship. Lecture notes, original proof of the standard theorem. sources.title: MIT 18.211 Combinatorial Analysis, Lecture 27: Adjacency Matrices and The Matrix-Tree Theorem
sources.notes: Downloaded and read pages 1-2. No usable date. Proposition 2 is stated for multigraphs, directed or undirected. Proposition 3 proof is brief: it uses the path bound n-1 without proving the walk-to-path lemma. Symbols flattened in quotes.

sources.title: An introduction to graph theory (Text for Math 530, Spring 2022, Drexel University)
sources.notes: Downloaded v3 and read Section 2.9 (pp. 36-42) as text; not the whole 400-plus page text. In this version Definition 2.9.1 is stated for simple graphs; graph-sources.md describes his statements as multidigraph-general, which holds for later sections, not for 2.9.1 in v3. Page numbers from the running header. Not peer reviewed; lecture text.

sources.title: Important Properties and Applications of the Adjacency Matrix (20250310)
sources.notes: Read pages 1-2. Theorem 2 is stated correctly but its proof is only a sketch, and sentence 4 of the sketch says (I + A)^(n-1) aggregates all paths of length at most n-1, which is incorrect for paths (it aggregates walks). No sum form A + ... + A^(n-1) appears in these notes.

sources.title: Properties of Adjacency Matrix of a Graph and It's Construction
sources.venue: Journal of Science, Eastern University, Sri Lanka (JSc EUSL), 12(1), pp. 13-21
sources.notes: Read the full 9-page PDF as text. Theorem 1 (p. 16) says the entry counts different paths, contradicted by the same paper's property 7 (p. 16) and by the proofs above. Theorem 2 (p. 17) is the sum form of the connectivity test; its proof sums path counts and does not use the walk-to-path lemma. Cite for the statement of the test only. Regional journal.

sources.title: CS 341: Algorithms, Module 3: breadth-first search, depth-first search (slides)
sources.notes: Read as text. Year not shown. This is the Module 3 slide deck, which is not the file graph-sources.md calls Lecture 10, so its slide numbers differ from that note. Slide 11 states the BFS correctness summary and lists testing connectivity as an application; the earlier slides argue correctness only in outline. Prove the connectivity step in the paper.

sources.title: compute.py: every matrix, sum, count and exhaustive check printed in the paper
sources.venue: Script in this repository, written by the paper's author
sources.notes: Run with python3 -I compute.py; output saved in appendices/compute.out. Pure Python integer arithmetic. Checks statements for small graphs; it is not a proof.

sources.title: m3_check.py: matrices and exhaustive connectivity check for module m3
sources.venue: Script in this repository, written by module owner m3
sources.notes: Run with python3 -I; output saved in modules/m3_check.out. Integer matrix multiplication, brute-force walk enumeration for k = 1 to 4, BFS, exhaustive over all labelled simple graphs with N = 1 to 6. Checks the statement for small N; it is not a proof.

contradictions.resolution: Paper proves the sum form itself using walk counting and the walk-to-path lemma.

contradictions.summary: Bai's sketch says (I + A)^(n-1) aggregates paths; Gotti's proof gets the same test through walks, the path bound, and the binomial identity. The test itself agrees in both; only the sketch sentence is wrong.
contradictions.resolution: Paper states the test, proves it via walks, and discusses the sketch sentence with a counterexample.

contradictions.summary: The textbook's path means no repeated edge (English trail) and its simple path means no repeated vertex; Grinberg and English usage call the latter path. The course convention follows the textbook's simple path.
contradictions.resolution: One three-column naming table; the paper writes simple path or course path and keeps the textbook's number beside each word.

contradictions.summary: Textbook Lemma 1.2.1 covers u different from v with no length bound; Grinberg Corollary 2.9.7 covers u = v and gives the bound k.
contradictions.resolution: Paper cites Lemma 1.2.1 for the course statement and Corollary 2.9.7 for the extended one, and proves the bound it uses.

contradictions.summary: Board drawing shows three lines; board matrix encodes two edges.
contradictions.resolution: Matrix is the example graph, per the brief; mismatch reported.
